podcasts.description:
Adversaries are already running AI agents, and the fastest attacks now play out in seconds. Sarah Guo and Elad Gil sit down with CrowdStrike president and CEO George Kurtz on what AI-equipped attackers mean for enterprise security. George explains how agents are flattening the adversary pyramid by putting advanced tradecraft in the hands of low-skill attackers, and why CrowdStrike and Nvidia are building a frontier-style lab of their own to train security models. They also get into how open-weight and closed models compare on security, where CrowdStrike is directing its platform investment, lessons from the recent Hugging Face incident, and why George sees AI, like every platform shift before it, as a net creator of opportunity.

podcasts.title: The Missing Infrastructure for AI Agents: Documents | Reducto’s Adit Abraham
podcasts.description:
AI agents can reason over enormous amounts of information, but much of the world’s actual work is still trapped in PDFs, spreadsheets, scans, and other formats that models struggle to reliably understand. Reducto co-founder and CEO Adit Abraham argues that solving this document layer is essential if agents are going to take on consequential work in healthcare, legal, finance, and insurance.

Adit joins a16z General Partner Jennifer Li to explain why traditional OCR breaks down on messy real-world documents, how Reducto combines vision-language models with specialized infrastructure to reach high accuracy without sacrificing cost or latency, and why frontier models can silently drop information on long extraction tasks. Reducto now processes billions of pages each month, including its seven billionth page the morning of the recording. 

They also discuss Reducto’s R1 model, agents that can review and correct their own document extraction, and the company’s push beyond simply reading files toward letting agents reliably work with and edit them. Underneath it all is a higher-stakes problem: when a misread word can affect a healthcare claim or financial decision, getting the input right matters just as much as making the model smarter.

podcasts.title: Sundar Pichai on Gemini 4 and putting data centers in space
podcasts.description:
Even Google can’t get enough compute. I sit down with Google and Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai shortly after the wider release of Gemini 4 Argon to discuss its early reception, where he still wants the model to improve, and what it takes to keep Google at the frontier of AI.

Pichai explains the recent leadership shakeup at Google DeepMind and why building frontier models has become an “all-consuming” job. We also get into Google’s answer to the personal agent race, how he predicts Gemini will do more work on your behalf, and whether agents will finally bring Search, Gmail, and Gemini together.

I ask him about Google turning free cash flow negative, the risks in the AI infrastructure buildout, and how he plans for demand years before knowing what the models will be capable of. He explains the signals giving him confidence to keep spending and how he uses AI agents to follow model development and compute usage inside Google.

We also discuss Project Suncatcher, Google’s new effort to put AI data centers in space, and why he thinks it belongs alongside bets like Waymo. He shares what’s next for Waymo and Wing, and when he expects quantum computing to become a real business.

podcasts.title: The Programmable Data Center — Evan Conrad, SF Compute
podcasts.description:
This was recorded on the sidelines of the new Compute Trading track at AIE NYC. Catch us next at AIE CODE, our last flagship for the top agentic engineers in the world.

In the early days of cloud, former guest Martin Casado made something so disruptive that Cisco was threatened enough to pay $600m for it, and VMware outbid for $1.3B:

That concept was software-defined networking, which virtualized the routing network by separating the control plane from the data plane. That revolution is now coming for GPUs - where previously running your own supercompute cluster required $50-100m upfront to get commitments and do the entire stack from hardware to firmware to kernels, SF Compute is now enabling you to not only buy or sell GPU hours now and in the future, but also to programmatically control everything from your network to memory.

We last spoke with Evan about commoditizing compute. At AI Engineer New York, we went deeper: what does it take to physically deliver a GPU contract, and what has to be true before a market in compute can become liquid?

From selling a room to running the hotel

Evan describes SF Compute’s expansion with a hotel analogy. A customer wants a room, then asks for cleaning, room service, and security. Eventually you discover that delivering the room means operating the hotel. podcasts.title: What Happens When Everyone Has a Health Expert in Their Pocket? | OpenAI’s Karan Singhal
podcasts.description:
More than 300 million people use ChatGPT for health and wellness questions each week. OpenAI’s Karan Singhal thinks that’s only the beginning: the longer-term goal is AI that can help people navigate their health proactively, while making trustworthy medical intelligence dramatically more accessible.

Karan joins a16z Partner Jay Rughani to explain why OpenAI trains healthcare expertise directly into its general-purpose frontier models, how it works with hundreds of medical experts to evaluate safety and disagreement, and why the company sees AI as a complement to doctors rather than a replacement for medical care. They also discuss integrations with Epic, AI copilots for clinicians, and what happens as personal agents begin navigating appointments, health records, and other fragmented parts of the healthcare system.

Looking further ahead, Karan makes the case that the cost of medical intelligence could continue to fall dramatically, allowing AI to act as a safety net for patients and clinicians, surface insights from years of health data, and potentially accelerate the discovery and validation of new treatments.

podcasts.title: FULL DISCUSSION: Nvidia Jensen Huang & German Merz Discuss AI, Robotics,Jobs, Germany’s Future |AC1E
podcasts.description:
FULL DISCUSSION: NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang joins German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on stage at the Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin for an in-depth discussion about artificial intelligence, industrial transformation, investment, manufacturing and Germany’s position in the global technology race.

Huang explains how AI, digital twins, robotics and autonomous vehicles could reshape factories and industrial production. He argues that Germany can build on its engineering expertise, manufacturing strength and industrial data to develop its own AI capabilities while benefiting from global technology.

The discussion also covers:
- Germany’s AI future: How AI could strengthen German manufacturing and industrial competitiveness.
- Digital twins and smart factories: Why future companies may operate both physical and digital factories.
- AI and employment: Huang’s view that AI can augment specialist knowledge rather than replace deep domain expertise.
- NVIDIA’s investment in Germany: Huang discusses the company’s investments, partnerships and support for German startups.
- AI regulation and safety: Huang outlines the roles of technology, industry best practices and government regulation.
- Europe’s global competitiveness: Merz discusses Germany’s ambitions to become a leading destination for industrial AI.
The conversation highlights the growing importance of AI, robotics, advanced manufacturing and investment as Germany seeks to strengthen its industrial future.

Watch the full discussion from Berlin’s Invest in Germany Summit.
